newsitem.title: UK: Dlr roars to 34-mth high, provoking Buba protests.
newsitem.headline: Dlr roars to 34-mth high, provoking Buba protests.

text.p: The dollar roared to its highest level in almost three years against the German mark here, prompting verbal protests from the Bundesbank which capped the unit just below 1.70 marks for now.

Dollar sentiment remains bullish, however. German economic gloom since news of another surge in jobless in January, and the relative buoyancy of the U.S. economy, are pushing interest rate expectations and yield spreads further in the dollar's favour.
Analysts argue that this fundamentally justifies a higher dollar and governments would be unwise to oppose this.

The news agency reported sources close to the German finance ministry advocating a rise in the dollar to between 1.70 and 1.75 marks. The dollar soared and set a 34-month high at 1.6935 marks in early European trade today.

The speed of the rise provoked the Bundesbank to issue an official statement. It said the news report was not the opinion held at the central bank and referred the market again to the G7's assertion that the dollar correction was over and that the communique was issued when the dollar was at 1.65 marks.
The German finance ministry said it had nothing to add to the G7 statement and its Japanese counterpart repeated its G7 line.
The Bundesbank response in particular sparked a sharp dollar retreat initially, helping many traders to lock in handsome profits made over the previous 24 hours.
At 1633 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6830/40 marks, up more than a pfennig from 1.6715/25 late Tuesday. Against the yen, it was at 123.80/85 compared with 122.75/85 late yesterday.
The dollar has risen 10.1 percent against the mark this year alone and is up 15.7 percent since last August.
"We got a much needed correction from the highs today but the medium-term targets are above 1.70 and probably onto 1.75," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America.
"There's bound to be some concern about the speed of the movement but most of Europe needs and is happy with a higher dollar," said Hawkins.

Shortly after the Bundesbank statement today, French finance minister Jean Arthuis said the dollar's rise reflects fundamentals and is favourable to French growth. While he cautioned against excess volatility, he said the inflationary impact of the higher dollar was "peanuts."
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin did little to dissuade dollar bulls. He reiterated that a strong dollar was in the U.S. interest and that the dollar has been strong for some time.
Outside the preceived devaluationist tendancies of single currency candidates in Europe, sterling again tracked the dollar higher and set a new 52-month high at 2.7685 marks.

The pound was aided by a bigger-than-expected 67,800 drop in UK unemployment in January, which like the recent U.S. employment report, contrasted sharply with the German picture and kept interest rate rise expectations on the boil.

The pound retreated after the Bundesbank statement, however, and was subdued when the Bank of England's quarterly inflation report appeared to soften its hardline stance on higher interest rates. --London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
